newsitem.title: FRANCE: Bomb and massacres kill 65 in Algeria.
newsitem.headline: Bomb and massacres kill 65 in Algeria.

text.p: A bomb ripped through an Algiers market crowded with women shoppers and children on Monday, killing 21 people and wounding about 40, Algerian security forces said.

The blast, blamed by Algerian security forces on Moslem militants, followed a weekend of massacres and kidnappings in villages in which 44 people, including 14 women and four adolescents, died, according to Algerian papers.
"I saw several heads that had been blown off, legs, arms and other limbs scattered in the area where the bomb exploded," one shocked resident told Reuters by telephone.
"It went off in the middle of the crowd of shoppers at the time the market was most busy. There were pools of blood everywhere."

The blast, the latest in a series of deadly explosions mainly in the Algerian capital, prompted Algiers' authorities on Monday to renew vows to clamp tight security measures on the city to thwart more Moslem rebel attacks.
"The security rules should be posted everywhere in shops and other public places," said Algerian radio quoting an official from the Algiers' governor's office.

The fresh security measures, making it compulsory for officials in shops, markets, buses and other public places to carry out security checks on people and cars, had been loosly implemented since they were imposed on June 2.

Residents said the bomb went off by a clothes shop in "Cite Baraka" also known as Cite d'Urgence (Emergency City) because of the small dwellings built quickly to house people who came from the countryside in the heyday of industrialisation in the 1970s.
The Algerian state-run television showed pictures of shocked wounded people, mostly women and girls, in hospital beds comforted by Health Minister Yahia Gouidom.
"About 50 slightly wounded people were given first aid at the small clinic nearby. Others, those badly wounded, were moved to Algiers main hospital," one resident added.
"Most of the dead are women and children," another said.
The explosion followed a bloody weekend reported by two leading Algerian papers.
In those attacks at least 44 people were killed, their throats slit or being hacked to death, and 21 young girls from one village were dragged off by rebels, probably to serve as "temporary brides".
Since June 5, when Algeria held a general election which officials hoped would help end more than five years of killings, around 400 people have died, according to Algerian newspapers.
One member of parliament told the assembly last week the toll was around 1,000 dead.
Last Wednesday, a bomb wounded 20 people watching a show in Le Musset Cinema in Belouizdad, a central district of Algiers.
El Watan daily said on Monday about 20 rebels attacked Fetha hamlet, near Ksar el Boukhari in Saturday-Sunday night.
They killed 33 members of five families, including 14 women and four adolescents, the well-informed paper, said.
Algeria's main Arabic language daily El Kbabar said the rebels used knives or axes to kill the villagers and then dragged away with them 21 young girls.
El Khabar said seven more people were killed on Saturday in a nearby village, Douar Aziz, and four more in Douar Barague in Ksar el Boukhari area, some 100 km (60 miles) from Algiers.
There was no official confirmation of the reports but security experts say the fact the heavily controlled newspapers carry them is seen as tacit confirmation.
About 60,000 people have been killed in Algeria's violence since 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which Islamists took a huge lead.
